section.title: Make growth explicit, adapt your coaching, and remove friction
section.deck: Laurent connects candid career alignment, fair evaluation, sustainable team leadership, and whole-problem ownership across Airbnb, Instagram, and Stripe.

blocks.question: Why did you choose to join Airbnb?
answer: Laurent had worked at Apple and Meta and decided developer productivity was the area he cared about: making engineers more effective at writing software. Moving to San Francisco turned his existing commute into roughly ninety minutes each way, which prompted a search. Airbnb combined people he liked, an office he could walk to, and a developer-infrastructure organization early enough to offer substantial work to shape.

He joined as one of two test-infrastructure engineers just as the broader effort was becoming multiple teams. The choice combined everyday quality of life with a technical opportunity; it was not a purely title-driven move.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: Why transition from test-infrastructure IC work into management?
answer: One manager was responsible for several teams and more than fifteen people, leaving limited time for development and support. Laurent had already begun doing some of that work as tech lead. As his team grew toward six to eight engineers, many early in their careers, he thought a dedicated manager could support them better and improve delivery of the large project.

He pitched the need to his manager and offered to try the role with help. He began with two reports and later managed the whole team. His rationale was an organizational problem he could help solve, rather than management as the automatic reward for technical seniority.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

followups.question: Did managing former peers create uncomfortable power dynamics?
answer: Yes, so they addressed them openly. A colleague used the first one-to-one to test his judgment: recruiting had said an employee missed an assigned interview, so what would the new manager do? Laurent said he would first ask what had happened and establish the facts. The colleague considered that a pass; immediately punishing the employee would ignore possibilities such as a mistaken name or inaccurate email.
The anecdote illustrates hearing all sides before acting. Formal authority does not eliminate the need to investigate or earn trust with people who were previously peers.
followups.speaker: Laurent

followups.question: How many managers would fail that test?
answer: He does not supply a percentage. Instead he criticizes treating management as one fixed style—tough, hands-off, or micromanaging. A directive approach may help a team of beginners and fail with experienced engineers. Good management requires adapting to the people and situation.
followups.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: How did management change your experience of boredom at work?
answer: He treats boredom as a signal to examine what is wrong rather than simply tolerate it. Becoming a manager initially supplied intense learning: hiring levels, reviews, promotions, then building relationships and planning reports’ growth. Later he used his optimization instincts to improve the team’s working conditions.

He built a calendar tool to reduce fragmentation across his own and reports’ schedules. He also surveyed every team process in detail—meetings, planning, code review, and ways of working—to improve team health. The survey showed that everyone thought the long stand-up was useful for someone else, while no one actually benefited much from it. Changing that and other processes improved engagement and enabled more work with less time.

After a three-week wedding trip, he returned to find the team had planned the next quarter and assignments using the process they had established. That successful independence also left him bored. The next possible step was managing managers, but he did not feel ready and missed coding, shipping, and seeing the effect in production. He returned to IC work. The story frames a well-functioning team as success even when its manager then wants a different challenge.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: Did learning management make you a better IC afterward?
answer: Yes. Understanding reviews, career framing, progression, and promotion helped him navigate his own work, while coaching and difficult-conversation skills improved his leadership of others. He continued developing those abilities after returning to IC work. The benefit was a new set of skills rather than merely privileged knowledge of a committee.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: Is pitching the organizational value a good way to move into management?
answer: He broadens the lesson to alignment with a manager. People often hesitate to say they want promotion, expertise, or another kind of growth, then present a year’s activity at review time and hope for the desired result. He prefers an ongoing conversation that gives both employee and manager the chance to shape the work.

As a manager he used a “surprise factor” exercise: before delivering the review, each person wrote the expected rating and promotion result, and they compared that with his own written assessment. Agreement was the desired outcome. He got close to full agreement without reaching it. The purpose was reducing uncertainty and demonstrating whether communication during the year had been effective.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

followups.question: Can a positive review surprise also reveal a problem?
answer: Yes. Someone doing excellent work without knowing it may be unnecessarily cautious. A manager should have coached that person toward greater confidence and productive risk-taking earlier rather than leave them anxious until an unexpected promotion. Positive surprises, like negative ones, can reveal missed communication.
followups.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: When should ICs try management, and what are the tradeoffs?
answer: Laurent found the experience invaluable and encourages people who are considering it to try. It is a different job, so direct experience can reveal both useful skills and whether the role fits. Even a poor outcome can teach something about one’s preferences and limitations.

He recommends starting with an intern while warning that one intern is a highly biased sample. Interns often need more direction and inspire strong personal attachment, unlike a group of experienced ICs. He recalls emotionally difficult intern calibrations because mentors strongly wanted their own intern to succeed and confused a return offer with proof of good management. A manager can do a good job even when the correct decision is no return offer. He helped run calibration sessions to make that distinction clearer and the process less frightening.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: Were your own promotions and reviews free of surprises?
answer: He first says he was often surprised, then clarifies that the surprises were ratings rather than promotions. He sees that as evidence he had not understood the system and its values well enough. In one transition, he expected his technical leadership to support a staff promotion but switched into management near the end of the cycle.

The rating came back as meets expectations because he had spent too little time in the new role. He found that frustrating and redirected his effort toward reaching the next management level. He now thinks he should have explicitly asked beforehand how the timing of a role change would affect review and promotion.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

followups.question: Did the role change reset your progression?
answer: He does not give a universal reset rule. Companies, organizations, and even local teams can develop informal calibration rules about tenure, role transitions, or unusually fast promotions. Some later become codified and communicated; others remain unstated until someone asks.

As a manager he challenged rules he found demotivating or inconsistent with the intended values and tried to explain calibration transparently to ICs. His bar was that an employee unexpectedly observing the meeting should be proud of the work, not feel that unfair decisions were being plotted. Because he sees management as representing company interests, strong value alignment was necessary for him to defend the decisions sincerely.
followups.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: How can a manager or IC successfully challenge an established rule?
answer: He starts by examining the biases a process may introduce and what makes employee evaluation fair. Gather evidence, understand the reason behind the rule, and make a case. The history may reveal a useful constraint you did not see—or an old precedent that no longer fits.

He generally prefers initial one-to-one conversations to a public confrontation in calibration. In front of a group, people can interpret disagreement as a threat to reputation and become defensive. Understanding those human dynamics improves the chance of changing the process rather than just winning an argument.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

followups.question: What if a senior leader proposes penalizing people for a low count of code changes?
answer: He would first clarify what the penalty and metric actually mean. Different contributions make lines of code or pull-request counts a poor general measure of engineering output. At Stripe, concerns about that kind of measurement motivated a more useful inquiry into the journey of a code change: thinking, writing, CI, review, iteration, and merge.

Time spent in different stages can reveal organizational friction. If one area takes twice as long to land changes, investigate why—perhaps a poor codebase or inefficient process. He explicitly rejects equating fast shipping with high productivity or slow shipping with low value. The metric is a diagnostic signal that helps remove obstacles, while a manager must assess the complete contribution, including noncoding work.
followups.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: What stood out about Airbnb’s engineering culture?
answer: He found it harder to explain why low-level infrastructure mattered in a designer-led company, but that different professional perspective also produced useful ideas. During a period of reliability problems, the company drew on people with emergency-response backgrounds to improve crisis management.

He admired the rigor and practices that resulted and took some to later jobs. His positive example is the willingness to ask which other field already handles a similar kind of problem well, rather than assuming all incident-management expertise must originate inside software engineering.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: Why return from Airbnb to Meta?
answer: After four years, the original stock grant’s vesting cliff affected earning potential, which was one reason to consider a move. He also thought he wanted to be an infrastructure generalist after working across testing, compute, databases, and other areas. He later decided that self-description was wrong, but it led him to Instagram at the time.

A disruptive July Fourth on-call experience prompted him to pursue reliability improvements. He knew Facebook already had tools addressing patterns Instagram still suffered from. He pitched adopting and partnering around that infrastructure to his skip-level manager and joined the resulting cross-organization project.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

followups.question: How did you find the right Facebook partners and gain buy-in?
answer: He was paired with a Facebook-side IC whom he regards as an exceptional technical leader. She brought the right people into discussions and secured the Facebook-side alignment. He credits her role rather than suggesting he independently knew and persuaded every partner.
followups.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: How did you choose a mentor, and what makes coaching useful?
answer: He sought people who were thoughtful, direct, able to challenge him, and capable of changing his mind in a way he could engage with. Those traits need not belong only to engineers; he sees them in his current coach too.

The Facebook-side collaborator had those qualities and helped him examine where his problem framing was wrong. A useful measure of coaching is whether the person actually changes how they think and act afterward, rather than repeating the same behavior. Although the host asks about his explicit mentorship pitch, the answer mainly explains selection and value; it does not provide a detailed script for making that request.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: What were your first impressions of Stripe?
answer: He encountered strong engineers, as he had in other jobs, and especially valued the emphasis on collecting and analyzing data before deciding. He considered its metrics-and-experimentation culture even stronger than the Meta culture he knew. That judgment is his personal comparison. It suited his own enjoyment of measuring progress and success.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: How did your technical-lead role grow across a much larger developer-infrastructure organization?
answer: He joined to lead build, test, and tooling across roughly thirty-five engineers, in areas he knew well. His first task was gaining credibility with people who already understood the local systems. He deliberately avoided citing his previous employer as automatic proof that a design should be copied or rejected.

Instead, he embedded with teams for about a month on concrete work, learned their rhythm, and asked questions that helped people reconsider decisions themselves. He made an exception for urgent incident response, where direct instructions could be necessary. Over a year he worked across most parts of the group and met the people repeatedly.

Leading a larger organization also meant accepting that each specialist knew more about their own domain than he did. He could guide with a broad developer-productivity perspective without pretending to be the local expert everywhere. Later he took two-to-eight-week assignments with different people or teams to bootstrap work and make it sustainable. Documentation and automation should allow the work to continue without requiring his constant presence or interrupting vacations. Being the sole keeper of secrets was the opposite of success.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: How did you scale yourself across so many engineers?
answer: Set realistic expectations: no leader of seventy people can know every current project in detail. Maintain contacts who can supply information, and be willing to say that you do not know yet and will return with an answer by a stated date. He believes confident misinformation damages trust much more than candid uncertainty; his emphatic career warning expresses that concern rather than a literal rule applying to every mistake.

He used office hours instead of attempting weekly meetings with everyone, providing enough capacity that people could get time within the week. Because about half the group was in Europe, he shifted his schedule to begin around five-thirty in the morning and create overlap with both European and American colleagues. Scaling still required direct communication and accessible help, just through a different structure.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: What do coaches commonly get wrong?
answer: They identify with a single style—hands-off, highly directive, or hint-based—and apply it to everyone. Laurent instead uses the person’s mastery, confidence, motivation, and immediate situation to choose the help. In his early Facebook onboarding work, three of four mentees progressed normally while one stalled; learning a situational-leadership model helped him adjust and unlock that person’s performance.

He describes moving from direction for a beginner, to encouragement and shared decision-making, to support, and finally delegation as skill develops. The assessment is specific to a skill and situation. A technically capable person can still need explicit help with something unfamiliar. A tired parent calling at four in the morning about an iPhone problem needs clear steps, not generic praise or a lecture on systems. Choosing only the supportive stage leaves many other needs unmet.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

followups.question: What specifically went wrong with the stalled boot-camp mentee?
answer: Laurent assumed every newcomer belonged in the same low-skill, high-motivation starting stage. This person had already studied the documentation extensively, knew more than the others in some areas, but had lost confidence and motivation. Repeated direction interrupted rather than supported learning.

After listening to what the mentee had done, he offered less prescriptive advice and more support. Performance improved sharply. The correction came from assessing the individual’s actual state, not applying more of the same technique with greater intensity.
followups.speaker: Laurent

blocks.title: Adjust coaching to developing capability

steps.title: Direct
steps.text: Give concrete steps when the skill is unfamiliar.

steps.title: Encourage and explain
steps.text: Support motivation and difficult choices as knowledge grows.

steps.title: Support
steps.text: Let the learner own decisions while providing help.

steps.title: Delegate
steps.text: Step back when the person can handle the work.

blocks.caption: Editorial synthesis of Laurent’s description. Arrows show a possible change in support as a particular skill develops; the actual choice also depends on motivation and the immediate situation.

blocks.question: Why can the senior-to-staff transition feel harder than the next transition?
answer: He sees a mindset change at staff: independently find the problem, choose and pitch it, solve it end to end, explain the result, and document it. Senior engineers can be strong designers and implementers while still working on problems identified by someone else.

In his model, later levels continue that complete cycle with larger scope rather than introduce the same fundamental autonomy shift again. This is his account of the distinction, not an assertion that later promotions are easy or mechanically determined.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: How can someone stuck at senior begin finding staff-level problems?
answer: Laurent channels frustration with real workflows. In developer productivity, each awkward command, window, delay, or repeated manual task can expose an opportunity. Stripe’s friction logs institutionalized that observation: work through a flow, record the steps with images, and ask why each action or loading screen exists.

He could identify dozens of possible improvements during a code change, then group related problems, rank them, and address the valuable ones. The goal is not merely collect annoyances. Look for families whose removal improves the overall experience. He also imagines a tired user: where would that person get confused, stuck, or drop off?

He applies the same habit beyond software. Repeated business travel can be an opportunity to refine the process each time until the twentieth trip is smoother than the first. The staff habit is continually learning from use, identifying friction, and deliberately improving it.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: Which book most influenced your career?
answer: He names Kim Scott’s Radical Candor, which helped him handle difficult conversations while building trust, motivating, and coaching reports. He appreciated its explanation of the manager-employee relationship and ideas he thinks many experienced managers still miss. This is his personal recommendation grounded in his transition, not an external review of the book.
blocks.speaker: Laurent

blocks.question: What would you tell yourself at the beginning of your career?
answer: The field changes even faster than it appears. Laurent contrasts interview practices he encountered early—such as estimation puzzles—with much more technical and monitored interviews he observes in the interview’s 2025 context. The examples illustrate change rather than establish a universal hiring policy.

He recommends staying curious and regularly reading technical news and discussions. He follows highly ranked weekly Hacker News items and has used that habit throughout his career. He expects the skills and experience of software engineering to keep changing substantially and would encourage his younger self to remain attentive rather than assume the original model of the job will persist.
blocks.speaker: Laurent
